item.title: Quantification of Large Language Model Distillation
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Quantification of Large Language Model Distillation [1] (ACL 2025), Sunbowen Lee, Junting Zhou, and Chang Ao, with corresponding authors Min Yang, Yitao Liang, Zhoufutu Wen, and Shiwen Ni (Chinese Academy of Sciences, Peking University, and others), propose two metrics for estimating how much one model was distilled from another and apply them to a dozen well-known LLMs.

Model distillation is a fundamental technique in building large language models (LLMs), transferring knowledge from a teacher model to a student model. However, distillation can lead to model homogenization, reducing diversity among models and impairing their ability to robustly handle complex or novel tasks. These limitations underscore the need to systematically quantify the distillation process and its impact. In this work, we propose a framework to evaluate and quantify model distillation. Our method addresses two key aspects: (1) Identifying identity cognition contradictions to assess discrepancies in how models perceive and represent identity-related information, and (2) Analyzing multi-granularity response similarities across models to measure the extent of homogenization. Experimental results demonstrate two key insights: (1) Well-known closed-source and open-source LLMs usually exhibit high distillation degrees, except for Claude, Doubao, and Gemini. (2) Base LLMs show higher distillation degrees compared to aligned LLMs. By offering a systematic approach to improve the transparency of LLM data distillation, we call for LLMs with more independent development and more transparent technical reports to improve LLMs’ robustness and safety.

Methods

The framework defines two metrics, each targeting a different trace distillation leaves behind. Figure 2 lays them out side by side: identity leakage on the left, response similarity on the right.

  • Identity Consistency Evaluation (ICE) measures whether a model leaks a false identity under pressure:
    • GPTFuzz [2], an open-source jailbreak framework, evolves adversarial prompts through an MCTS-guided search that mutates jailbreak templates until they get past a model’s self-identity guardrails.
    • A judge model (GPT-4o-mini) then checks whether the answer contradicts a fixed fact set describing the model’s real identity (for example, “I am Claude, an AI assistant developed by Anthropic”).
    • The identity prompts span five categories: team, cooperation, industry, technology, and geography.
    • Each score is the share of jailbreak attempts that produce a contradiction, so a higher score means more identity leakage and, by the paper’s reasoning, a higher degree of distillation. The three variants differ only in what counts as a contradiction, from loosest to strictest:
      • Loose counts any identity contradiction.
      • Strict counts only responses that claim to be another named model such as Claude or GPT.
      • Hard counts a leak only when the prompt itself contains no identity keywords but the response does, ruling out cases where the jailbreak prompt fed the model the name it echoed back.
  • Response Similarity Evaluation (RSE) measures how closely a test model’s answers track a reference model’s. A judge model scores each test response against the reference (GPT-4o-0806) on response style, logical structure, and content detail, using a five-level similarity scale, averaged over three prompt sets: ArenaHard, NuminaMath, and ShareGPT.

The two metrics are meant to be read together: ICE catches the categorical tell of distillation (a model that thinks it is a different model), while RSE captures the graded one (a model whose answers have drifted toward the reference’s shape). Both route the actual judgment through an LLM-as-a-judge rather than a fixed string match.

Results

The two metrics run on overlapping but distinct model sets. ICE probes eight instruction-tuned models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Doubao-Pro-32k, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Llama 3.1 70B-Instruct, Phi-4, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-Max-0919, and GLM-4-Plus) with 50 seed jailbreak prompts evolved by GPTFuzz and scored by GPT-4o-mini. RSE covers twelve models against the GPT-4o-0806 reference on 1,000-example subsets of each dataset, with n-gram overlap and BERTScore [3] reported alongside as word-level baselines. To check the judge, the authors hand-labeled 100 sampled cases per condition, and human and LLM verdicts agree in the mid-to-high 0.9s on negatives and 0.78–0.90 on positives (Table 1).

The findings:

  • Claude and Doubao barely leak, while the newer Chinese frontier models leak most. On ICE, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Doubao-Pro-32k produce almost no contradictory identity responses (Hard Score near 0), while GLM-4-Plus, Qwen-Max-0919, and DeepSeek-V3 score highest (GLM-4-Plus reaches Loose 0.42, Hard 0.16), as the cover chart shows.
  • Qwen-Max repeatedly self-identifies as Claude. In 32% of its Strict-Score samples, Qwen-Max-0919’s jailbroken responses reference Claude, sometimes near-verbatim (“an AI assistant created by Anthropic to be helpful, harmless, and honest”).
  • Base models leak more than their aligned versions. Qwen-2.5 base scores around 0.2 on Strict where the Instruct counterparts score near 0.00, and Llama 3.1 base scores 0.288 against Instruct’s 0.082 (Table 3). Alignment scrubs the identity signal that pretraining picked up.
  • The leak concentrates in team, industry, and technology questions. Across the five identity-prompt categories, the contradictions cluster in team affiliation, industry, and technology rather than cooperation or geography, which the authors read as the areas where distilled training data was least filtered or anonymized [1].
  • RSE reproduces the same ordering, inside a tight range. Similarity to GPT-4o-0806 runs from Llama 3.1 70B (3.628), Doubao (3.720), and Claude (3.740) at the low end up to DeepSeek-V3 (4.102), Qwen-Max (4.174), and GPT-4o-0513 (4.240) at the high end, out of 5.
  • RSE rises when a model is actually distilled. Fine-tuning Qwen-2.5-7B for three epochs on the reference model’s outputs lifts its RSE score at every epoch (Table 5), and within the DeepSeek-R1 distillation series the larger students resemble the teacher more than the smaller ones do.

The whole ranking falls between 3.6 and 4.2: every model scores fairly close to GPT-4o, so the distillation signal is in the ordering rather than the absolute number. The GPT-series entry (GPT-4o-0513) tops the non-reference field, and the models the authors call low-distillation (Claude, Doubao, Llama) cluster at the bottom of the same metric that ICE flags them low on.

References

  1. Lee, Sunbowen, Zhou, Junting, Ao, Chang, Li, Kaige, Du, Xinrun, He, Sirui, Wu, Haihong, Liu, Tianci, Liu, Jiaheng, Alinejad-Rokny, Hamid, Yang, Min, Liang, Yitao, Wen, Zhoufutu, Ni, Shiwen. “Quantification of Large Language Model Distillation.” ACL 2025 (arXiv:2501.12619), January 22, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12619
  2. Yu, Jiahao, Lin, Xingwei, Yu, Zheng, Xing, Xinyu. “GPTFuzzer: Red Teaming Large Language Models with Auto-Generated Jailbreak Prompts.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2309.10253), September 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10253
  3. Zhang, Tianyi, Kishore, Varsha, Wu, Felix, Weinberger, Kilian Q., Artzi, Yoav. “BERTScore: Evaluating Text Generation with BERT.” ICLR 2020 (arXiv:1904.09675), April 2019. https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09675

Related Posts

  • DeepSeek vs ChatGPT on Ethical Questions: an earlier read where a DeepSeek/ChatGPT behavioral gap could not be traced to pretraining versus output-based tuning, the same identification limit these two metrics run into.
  • Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Reactivates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books: finds three providers memorize the same passages in the same places, independent evidence that frontier models share a training substrate rather than copy each other directly.
  • How Far Behind the Closed Frontier Are Open-Weights LLMs?: treats distillation as the late-mover advantage that closes the coding gap fastest, the same efficiency shortcut whose footprint this paper tries to measure.

item.title: Japan’s Top Court Rules AI Can’t Be a Patent Inventor
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

The Yomiuri Shimbun reports that Japan’s Supreme Court has dismissed an American engineer’s appeal to have an AI named as the inventor on a patent application, finalizing that an inventor under the Patent Law must be a natural person.

What the article reports:

  • The application. A 2020 filing for food containers and other items named the inventor as “DABUS, the artificial intelligence that autonomously invented this invention.” The Patent Office ordered the applicant to supply a person’s name. When the plaintiff refused, the application was rejected.
  • The lower courts. The plaintiff argued that “patent applications even for inventions created by AI should be accepted.” The Tokyo District Court held that the Patent Law “presumes that an inventor is a natural person,” and the Intellectual Property High Court agreed, restricting inventors to “natural persons.”
  • The high court’s caveat. The high court added that the law “had not anticipated the rapid development of AI,” and that whether patent rights should extend to AI-created inventions “would require discussion given the impact this would have on society.”
  • The final ruling. In a decision dated March 4, 2026, the Supreme Court’s Second Petty Bench turned down the engineer’s appeal to overturn the Patent Office’s rejection, finalizing the lower-court rulings.

My Notes

  • DABUS is a coordinated test case run across jurisdictions, and Japan now sides with the majority: its creator Stephen Thaler has filed the same AI-inventor claim in multiple countries to force the question, and Japan joins the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Patent Office in holding that an inventor must be a human. Only South Africa granted the patent, so the rulings are close to a global consensus that existing patent law reads “inventor” as a person.

  • The courts settled the statute and left the policy question to lawmakers: the ruling resolves only that current law reads “inventor” as a natural person, and the high court’s remark that the law “had not anticipated” AI concedes that whether rights should extend to AI-created inventions is a question for the Diet, Japan’s legislature.

  • The ruling leaves open what happens to an invention with no eligible human inventor: the campaign is really testing that, not whether an AI can hold a patent. Thaler’s refusal to name himself is strategic, so this rejection is partly self-inflicted. But when an invention genuinely has no human to name as inventor, the natural-person rule makes it unpatentable by anyone, and leaving a whole class of inventions unprotected is a policy choice in its own right.

  • Patent and copyright are converging on the same rule: copyright law already holds that AI output with no human author gets no protection, as when a US federal judge held AI-generated art cannot be copyrighted in another Thaler case. With both regimes denying protection where no human is involved, the incentive question shifts toward whoever built or operated the system rather than the system itself.

Related Posts

  • AI-Generated Art Cannot Be Copyrighted, Rules a US Federal Judge: the copyright analogue, same plaintiff pattern and the same human-authorship requirement.
  • US Copyright Office Guidance on Generative AI: the administrative version of the human-contribution line these court rulings draw.
  • Copyright Office Seeks Public Input on AI Protections and Liability: the “leave it to policymakers” move the Japanese high court echoes.
  • Northwestern Symposium on Law + Computation: the broader law-and-computation frame these AI-authorship disputes sit inside.

item.title: How to Mimic Elite Runner Mechanics
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Runner’s World collects the biomechanics research on why elite runners look effortless, and it makes a claim I find more useful than the usual “run more” advice: the gap is mostly about where the propulsive force comes from and how little time the foot spends on the ground, rather than raw fitness.

The article’s account of the elite–amateur gap breaks into four linked mechanisms, in the order the piece presents them:

  • Propulsion originates in the calves. Scott Delp (Stanford bioengineering) names the gastrocnemius and soleus as the biggest contributors to upward and forward propulsion, working through plantar flexion. A 2023 Frontiers in Sports and Active Living study found trained collegiate runners drew more of their power from the ankle than recreational runners, tracking with their faster speeds. In slower runners the knee does more of the work, so the quads dominate push-off, and quad-driven push-off adds a horizontal force directed backward that decelerates. The prescription is targeted calf work: calf raises and their variations.

  • Faster runners spend less time on the ground. Mike Hahn (University of Oregon) frames speed as the ability to exert force against the ground more quickly. A 2022 Bioengineering study found elite and experienced runners have a lower “duty factor,” less time with the foot down, while older work in the Journal of Applied Physiology found faster runners apply about 1.26 times the average ground force. A deep knee bend and ankle dorsiflexion make for a soft, spongy stride that wastes energy stabilizing the body. Shortening step length and raising cadence lands the foot under the body and gets it off the ground faster.

  • A stiff ankle behaves like a spring. A 2023 Frontiers in Physiology study found elites run “springier.” On landing, a stiff ankle stores and returns elastic energy, while a floppy one acts as a shock absorber and loses that return as the runner sinks into the quads. Plyometrics such as pogo jumps are cited as a proven way to build tendon stiffness.

  • The payoff is a longer aerial phase. A study in the European Journal of Sport Science compared elites and recreational runners at the same speed and found the main difference was neither stride length nor cadence but an 11% longer flight time. Elites dip less on landing and hold a higher, longer push-off, like a bouncing ball with a shallow dip and a pronounced rise. The article presents air time as the cumulative result of the other three mechanisms, earned through consistent training.

Related Posts

  • Temperature’s Effect on My Running Efficiency: another case where the running-efficiency metric I care about turned out to be downstream of a factor I couldn’t adjust directly.
  • The Easy Interval Method: Intervals Every Day, Run Easy: a training-structure counterpart to this piece’s form-and-mechanics angle on getting faster.
  • CoachGPT, in Practice: on handing training decisions to an AI coach, which is exactly the kind of system that could turn these mechanics into a prescribed plan.

item.title: The Future Worth Building Is Human
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Thinking Machines Lab published its manifesto: a case that AI should extend human will and judgment rather than race ahead on its own. The route it lays out is customizable models people can train on their own knowledge, live multimodal interaction, and alignment distributed across many owners instead of decided in a few labs.

The essay builds its case in four moves:

  • The mission and the four bets. The lab frames its purpose as building AI that “extends human will and judgment,” against a default where models are “trained in a handful of places and then frozen,” unshaped by the people they serve. It names four technical directions:

    • Train frontier models that advance multimodal interaction and customizability.
    • Build tools that let people make models their own, including “the ability to train model weights.”
    • Develop interfaces that widen the human–machine communication channel.
    • Publish research so the power to shape AI is broadly understood.

  • Bringing intelligence to knowledge. Productive know-how is tacit, local, and continuously updated (a chef refining a recipe, a shopkeeper rearranging a display), so it cannot be written into a database or captured by a model trained once and frozen, citing Michael Polanyi’s The Tacit Dimension and Friedrich Hayek’s The Use of Knowledge in Society on why central planning fails. Autonomous AI suffices only where the goal is static and expressible and no hidden knowledge exists, as in chess and math. Elsewhere AI must itself be distributed. The essay invokes Toyota’s 2014 decision to bring master craftsmen back onto the line (Mitsuru Kawai: “to be the master of the machine, you have to have the knowledge and the skills to teach the machine”) to argue intelligence and knowledge lift each other rather than substitute.

  • Human participation as a technical challenge. Today’s human–AI channel, “a small text box and a long wait,” is too narrow and slow for live collaboration, motivating a long-term bet on interaction models that handle live, multimodal interaction natively “in the model itself rather than in scaffolding bolted around it.” The essay critiques the dominant metric, METR’s time horizon of software tasks models execute autonomously, as measuring only what AI does alone rather than what people and machines accomplish together. It argues its incentives align: a lab selling one model to every customer benefits by absorbing what makes each user distinct, while the lab benefits when customers own and adapt models to their advantages.

  • Decentralized alignment. Values, like knowledge, resist consolidation, yet AI’s values are decided in a handful of places, and “a single locus of value alignment … becomes a locus of power to be captured.” It ties this to the concentration danger in The Intelligence Curse and cites Leo XIV’s Magnifica Humanitas (“a more moral AI is not enough if that morality is determined by a few”), noting each lab now trains its next flagship on the previous one’s outputs, so everyone inherits one character. Its fix is to encode values in user-owned weights rather than prompts: a prompt-only change leaves deeper habits intact, and a prompt-malleable central model is attack-vulnerable (Gwern’s Guardian Angels). It concedes, via von Neumann, that the power to shape a model for good is also the power to shape it for ill, and envisions alignment as an ecosystem of diverse AIs “raised in different places, disagreeing, competing, and learning from each other.”

  • The future worth building. Closing on Hannah Arendt’s The Human Condition, the essay rejects framing human involvement as a trade-off against capability or safety, casting participation, ownership, and diverse alignment as technical problems to solve rather than costs to pay: “the future is not a choice between human dominance and rapid obsolescence.”

My Notes

  • The whole case is a bet on tacit knowledge. Recast as model architecture, Hayek’s argument says knowledge is too tacit and local to freeze into one model. The essay’s own carve-out marks where that stops: autonomous AI is enough wherever a goal is static, expressible, and hides no knowledge, as in chess and math. The bet is that most valuable work stays outside that zone. As models improve and more goals turn out to be expressible, the zone may keep growing, and where the line settles decides how much of the case survives.

  • Distributing alignment also distributes the risk. The essay’s fix for a single locus of power, encoding values in user-owned weights rather than prompts, spreads the risk of misuse as widely as the power itself. It concedes a prompt-malleable central model is attack-vulnerable, but never resolves why widely distributed weights are safer rather than just differently exposed.

  • What keeps the lab competitive if customers own the weights? The essay argues its incentives are aligned: it benefits when customers own and adapt their own models rather than renting one. That is a candid business case, but it leaves a question unanswered: where the durable advantage comes from once the customer holds the weights.

    • The moat. Selling a model and handing over the weights gives away the asset other labs rent out. The four technical directions imply an answer (stay on the frontier, own the tooling and the interaction layer), but the essay does not spell out how those sustain a business when each customer’s real value lives in weights the lab no longer controls.
    • Portability. Weights are tied to an architecture. When the base model is replaced, especially if the architecture changes, a customer’s fine-tuned weights do not obviously transfer, and they may have to retrain each generation. Their data and training recipes survive the switch and can be reapplied to whatever model comes next.

Related Posts

  • Interaction Models: Training Real-Time Collaboration into the Model: the lab’s earlier technical piece on the live-interaction bet this essay builds on.
  • Magnifica Humanitas: Pope Leo XIV’s Encyclical on AI: a source the essay cites, sharing its concern about morality decided by a few.
  • The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal: the power-concentration danger the essay’s locus-of-power argument echoes.
  • Daron Acemoglu on AI, Jobs, and Liberal Democracy: a parallel case for distributing AI’s benefits rather than concentrating them.

item.title: AI and Job Postings: From Destruction to Creation?
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Indeed Hiring Lab reports a reversal: the occupations most exposed to AI, which fell hardest from 2022 to 2026, are now leading the rebound in job postings. US software-development postings are up almost 15% since Claude Code launched in late February 2025, while postings overall fell 7% over the same window.

What the report finds:

  • A software rebound off a low base. Since Claude Code’s late-February-2025 launch, the same month the term “vibecoding” was coined, US software-development postings on Indeed have risen almost 15%, while overall postings fell about 7%. But software still stands at index 72.5 (February 2020 = 100), about 27.5% below its pre-pandemic level, while overall postings are essentially flat at 101.4. The rebound is a change in slope well short of a recovery.
  • The rebound shows up across most rich economies. The software-development share of all postings is climbing in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia, with Germany and France the exceptions. Hiring Lab notes that the English-speaking countries have the most consistent gains, and reads that as possible earlier adoption of agentic-AI tools.
  • The AI-exposure relationship flipped. From May 2022 to May 2026, the more of an occupation’s skills generative AI could transform, the more its postings fell, a statistically significant if uncontrolled correlation, with declines that began before ChatGPT’s late-2022 release. Over the most recent year the slope reverses: higher AI exposure now predicts a larger rebound, and not only for software development.
  • The gains are senior and AI-fluent. 71% of the net rise in software-development postings from May 2025 to May 2026 came from senior roles (titles with senior, lead, principal, director, or manager) and 37% from titles mentioning AI (AI, machine learning, deep learning, or prompt). The two categories overlap. Hiring Lab reads this as demand for experienced people who can work with AI, consistent with prior evidence on AI’s disproportionate hit to entry-level jobs.
  • Hiring Lab’s read: destruction turning to creation. It describes the shift as AI exposure moving from job destruction toward job creation, with AI mentions in titles now spreading beyond software into other white-collar occupations. The report stresses that correlation is not causation, treats the Claude Code timing as a coincidence it declines to over-read, and argues the future of work depends on how the exposure-versus-postings slope evolves.

My Notes

  • The rebound favors AI-augmented senior roles. The net gain is concentrated in senior and AI-titled work, so what looks like job creation is closer to AI augmenting experienced developers, the augment-over-replace case in Daron Acemoglu on AI, Jobs, and Liberal Democracy, than to genuinely new demand for software.

  • Entry-level hiring keeps shrinking. The net gain is in senior roles, while payroll data shows early-career software developers still contracting: The AI Entry-Level Jobs Effect Isn’t Fading put workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed jobs down about 3.8% a year.

  • The same exposure metric now predicts rebounds. Indeed’s GenAI-exposure score marked the occupations that fell most through 2026 and now marks those rebounding most: exposure flags which occupations swing hardest, in either direction. The direction depends on the tool era and flipped when agentic tools arrived, a caution against treating any exposure measure, including the one in GPTs Are GPTs: Labor Market Impact of Large Language Models, as a one-way forecast.

Related Posts

  • Daron Acemoglu on AI, Jobs, and Liberal Democracy: the augmentation-versus-displacement debate this data speaks to directly.
  • GPTs Are GPTs: Labor Market Impact of Large Language Models: the occupation-exposure measurement this rebound is read against.
  • Who Will Actually Thrive in the Hybrid AI-Human Work Force?: the senior, AI-fluent worker the rebound favors.
  • The AI Entry-Level Jobs Effect Isn’t Fading: payroll evidence that early-career, AI-exposed employment keeps shrinking even as senior postings recover.
  • Anthropic Economic Index: another attempt to measure AI’s real footprint in the labor market.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Has Landed
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Artificial Analysis ran OpenAI’s new GPT-5.6 family through its pre-release evaluations. The top model, Sol, scores one point below Claude Fable 5 on the Intelligence Index at roughly a third of the cost, and the family fills out a new price-versus-intelligence frontier below it. Sol also tops the new Coding Agent Index at 80. Terra and Luna sit below Sol at progressively lower cost.

The family comes in three tiers. Sol is the flagship, the most capable and most expensive, at $5/$30 per million input/output tokens. Terra is the mid tier at $2.5/$15, and Luna the smallest and cheapest at $1/$6. All three are reasoning models with selectable effort, and GPT-5.6 adds a new max setting above the previous top. Raising the effort spends more tokens for more intelligence.

What the Benchmarks Show

  • Intelligence Index: Sol (max) scores 59, one point behind Fable 5 (60) and ahead of Opus 4.8 (56). Terra and Luna score 55 and 51. On the new Coding Agent Index, Sol leads at 80, with Terra and Luna at 77 and 75.

  • Cost: Sol reaches near-parity at $1.04 per Intelligence Index task, about a third of Fable 5’s $2.75 and below Opus 4.8’s $1.80. Terra and Luna cost $0.55 and $0.21. Across reasoning-effort settings the family defines a new intelligence-versus-cost Pareto frontier, and each model beats GPT-5.5. Luna and Sol sit ahead of Terra at every effort level, so no Terra setting is worth choosing over the matching Luna or Sol one.

  • Coding Agent Index (new): the index pairs each model with an agentic harness and averages three evaluations: DeepSWE, Terminal-Bench v2, and SWE-Atlas-QnA. Sol in Codex leads all three (tying Grok 4.5 in Grok Build on SWE-Atlas-QnA) at $7.08 per task, roughly 40% and 10% under Fable 5 and Opus 4.8 in Claude Code.
  • Token use: Sol (max) spends 15k output tokens per task, just under GPT-5.5’s 16k and well under Opus 4.8 (41k) and Claude Sonnet 5 (69k) while scoring higher, defining a new intelligence-versus-tokens frontier.
  • Knowledge work (AA-Briefcase): on this agentic knowledge-work benchmark Sol ranks second to Fable 5 and posts the highest Presentation Elo of any model (1656), but Fable 5 keeps the top spot on Rubric Score (56% vs 42%) and Analytical Quality Elo (1764 vs 1592).
  • Economically valuable tasks (GDPval-AA v2): Sol (1748) essentially ties Fable 5 (1760), both far above the 1,000 human baseline.

  • Knowledge reliability (AA-Omniscience): Sol edges past GPT-5.5 on accuracy (59%), but its hallucination rate climbs to 89%.

  • Cache-write pricing: GPT-5.6 keeps OpenAI’s 90% cache-read discount but is the first OpenAI family to charge for cache writes, at 1.25x the input price, matching Anthropic.

My Notes

  • Cost is the deciding variable now. When the top model trails Fable 5 by a single Intelligence Index point, quality stops driving the choice and price does. Sol’s lower cost comes partly from spending fewer output tokens, and per-task cost climbs with the tokens each turn re-sends, the growth law The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents derives.

  • The coding lead is model-plus-harness. Sol’s 80 is measured in Codex, OpenAI’s own harness, and the index pairs each model with a harness by design, so the ranking credits the pairing. A different harness moves both the score and the per-task cost, an effect Databricks measured directly on its own codebase, which makes a cross-model coding claim hard to read as a statement about the model by itself.

  • Cache-write pricing is the structural change. The new cache-write charge is a small line item, but it reprices long-context agentic workloads, which write large prompts to cache on nearly every turn. It also puts a price on the memory that agentic inference leans on, the resource The Inference Shift argues becomes the binding constraint once no human is waiting on the model.

  • These are pre-release numbers. Artificial Analysis discloses that it ran the evaluation before launch in coordination with OpenAI. The scores still come from a third party running its own index, and the pre-release arrangement is context worth having when reading them. How Artificial Analysis Builds Its Intelligence Index covers what the index does and does not capture.

Related Posts

  • How Artificial Analysis Builds Its Intelligence Index: the same source, explaining the methodology behind the numbers this report cites.
  • Benchmarking Coding Agents on Databricks’ Multi-Million-Line Codebase: independent evidence that harness choice moves per-task cost as much as model choice, on real internal tasks.
  • Claude Opus 4.8: The Early Reactions: the incumbent Sol is repeatedly measured against on both intelligence and cost.
  • The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents: the token-cost growth law behind why per-task cost climbs with usage.
  • The Inference Shift: the pricing and inference-economics backdrop for cache-write charges.
